title: S05 Knowledge Gate: Confluent Schema Registry & Data Contracts
description: Pre-Lab Conceptual Readiness Check for Schema Registry, Avro Wire Format, Magic Byte, Compatibility Modes, and Schema Evolution.

questions.question: What is the Confluent Schema Registry Wire Format prepended to every serialized Avro payload in Kafka?

options.B: 1 Magic Byte (`0x00`) followed by a 4-byte Big-Endian integer representing the Schema ID registered in Schema Registry.
options.C: The full JSON text of the Avro schema definition repeated in every message.
options.D: The sender's IP address and MAC address.

questions.diagnostic_hint: How many bytes are added to the beginning of the binary payload: 1 magic byte plus how many bytes for the schema integer ID?
questions.explanation: Confluent SerDe prefixes exactly 5 bytes to each payload: Byte 0 is the Magic Byte (`0x00`), and Bytes 1-4 encode the 32-bit Schema ID in big-endian network byte order. This allows consumers to extract the ID, fetch/cache the schema once, and deserialize payloads without embedding bulky schema definitions in every record.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect; Kafka wire format does not use string UUID prefixes.
option_explanations.B: Correct! Exactly 5 bytes (1 byte magic + 4 bytes schema ID) achieves 80%+ bandwidth efficiency over JSON.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect; embedding the full schema in every message is an anti-pattern that Schema Registry was specifically built to eliminate.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect; network metadata belongs to TCP/IP headers, not message bodies.

questions.question: Under `BACKWARD` compatibility mode (the default), what does the compatibility rule mandate?

options.A: New schemas can only be written by legacy producers.
options.B: Consumers using the NEW schema must be able to process events produced with the OLD schema (previous version).
options.C: Consumers using the old schema must be able to process new schema events.
options.D: All topic data must be deleted before registering a new schema.

questions.diagnostic_hint: Think of rollout order: if you upgrade consumers first, which schema version are consumers using, and which data are they reading?
questions.explanation: `BACKWARD` compatibility means consumers upgraded to Schema V(new) can deserialize data produced with Schema V(old). This allows upgrading consumers first before upgrading producers. Rules: (1) Fields can be deleted. (2) New fields MUST have a default value defined.

option_explanations.B: Correct! New consumer code successfully reads old historical event data.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect; that is the definition of `FORWARD` compatibility (upgrade producers first).
option_explanations.D: Completely false; schema evolution preserves historical log data.

questions.question: What happens if a developer attempts to register an INCOMPATIBLE schema version against a subject in Confluent Schema Registry? (Select ALL that apply)

options.A: Schema Registry rejects the registration and returns an `HTTP 409 Conflict` status code.
options.C: The producer attempting to register the breaking schema throws a `SchemaRegistryException` (or `IncompatibleSchemaException`).
options.D: Kafka formats the disk containing that topic.

questions.diagnostic_hint: What HTTP error code indicates schema compatibility failure? Does the broker crash?
questions.explanation: Schema Registry enforces data contracts at registration time. An incompatible schema is rejected with `HTTP 409 Conflict` (A), causing client SerDes to raise an exception (C). The Kafka broker cluster is completely unaffected (B), and no data is deleted (D).

option_explanations.A: True: Standard REST API rejection code for compatibility violations.
option_explanations.B: False: Schema Registry is an external service; brokers are not impacted.
option_explanations.C: True: Fail-fast exception in client application before sending invalid bytes.
option_explanations.D: False: Topics and logs remain completely intact.

questions.question: What is the consequence of adding a new field to an Apache Avro schema WITHOUT providing a `"default"` attribute in `BACKWARD` compatibility mode?

options.B: The new schema is rejected as incompatible because consumers using the new schema cannot deserialize older messages where that field does not exist.
options.C: The field is automatically filled with random numbers.
options.D: Avro converts all fields to string format.

questions.diagnostic_hint: If an old message does not contain the new field, how can a new consumer construct the object without a fallback default value?
questions.explanation: In `BACKWARD` compatibility, if a new consumer reads an old message, it looks for the new field in the payload. Since old records do not contain it, deserialization will fail unless the schema defines a `default` value (e.g. `"default": null` or `"default": "standard"`). Omitting the default causes Schema Registry to reject the evolution.

option_explanations.A: False: Schema validation is enforced, not bypassed.
option_explanations.B: Correct! Default values are mandatory for backward-compatible field additions.
option_explanations.C: False: Deserializers require deterministic types and values.

questions.question: Which of the following serialization formats are natively supported by modern Confluent Schema Registry? (Select ALL that apply)
questions.diagnostic_hint: Which three structured contract formats have official Confluent SerDe libraries?
questions.explanation: Confluent Schema Registry natively supports three enterprise data contract formats: (A) Apache Avro, (B) Protocol Buffers (Google Protobuf), and (C) JSON Schema. Plain CSV (D) is unstructured text without formal schema compatibility semantics.

option_explanations.A: Supported: The foundational binary format for Big Data and Hadoop/Spark ecosystems.
option_explanations.B: Supported: Google binary format widely used in gRPC microservices.
option_explanations.C: Supported: Standard declarative JSON contract format.
option_explanations.D: Unsupported: CSV lacks machine-enforceable contract and evolution semantics.

questions.question: By default, what naming strategy does Schema Registry use to associate schemas with topics for value payloads (`TopicNameStrategy`)?
questions.diagnostic_hint: If your topic is `retail.orders`, what is the subject name registered in Schema Registry for message values?
questions.explanation: Under `TopicNameStrategy` (the default), message values are registered under subject `<topic>-value` (e.g. `retail.orders-value`), and keys are registered under `<topic>-key`. This isolates value and key evolution per topic.

option_explanations.A: Correct! The standard Confluent subject convention for record payloads.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect; this is used for message keys, not values.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect; subjects are scoped per topic unless using `RecordNameStrategy`.

questions.question: Under `FULL` compatibility mode, what must be true for all schema changes? (Select ALL that apply)

options.B: Old consumers can read messages written by new producers, AND new consumers can read messages written by old producers.
options.C: Producers and consumers can be upgraded in ANY order (independently).
options.D: All fields must be marked as deprecated.

questions.diagnostic_hint: What is the advantage of combining Backward and Forward compatibility?
questions.explanation: `FULL` compatibility combines Backward and Forward. (A) It enforces bidirectional evolution. (B) Old and new clients can cross-communicate seamlessly. (C) It decouples team deployment schedules, allowing producers and consumers to roll out in any arbitrary order. (D) is false.

option_explanations.A: True: Both directional constraints are strictly enforced.
option_explanations.B: True: True bidirectional interoperability across client versions.
option_explanations.C: True: Independent deployment freedom across distributed engineering teams.
option_explanations.D: False: Deprecation is optional documentation, not a schema rule.

questions.question: Where does Confluent Schema Registry physically store registered schemas and subject version histories?

options.B: In an internal, compacted Kafka topic named `_schemas` within the Kafka cluster itself.
options.C: In text files on the local root filesystem.

questions.diagnostic_hint: Does Schema Registry depend on an external relational database, or does it 'eat its own dog food' by using Kafka?
questions.explanation: Schema Registry is a stateless Java application that stores all schemas, subject configurations, and metadata in a special compacted Kafka topic named `_schemas`. Multiple Schema Registry instances use this topic to achieve high availability and active-standby leader election without external database dependencies.

option_explanations.A: False: Schema Registry does not require relational databases.
option_explanations.B: Correct! The `_schemas` topic acts as a distributed, durable, replicated commit log for schema contracts.
option_explanations.C: False: Ephemeral local files would break clustering and container restarts.

questions.question: Why is client-side schema caching critical for Confluent Producer and Consumer performance?

options.A: Because Schema Registry charges per HTTP request.
options.B: Because without caching, every single message serialized or deserialized would require an HTTP network round-trip to Schema Registry, dropping throughput from 100,000 msgs/sec to under 100 msgs/sec.
options.C: Because Kafka brokers refuse messages without client certificates.
options.D: Because Avro requires cached schemas to calculate checksums.

questions.diagnostic_hint: What would happen to latency if every message required an HTTP REST call to port 8081?
questions.explanation: Client SerDes maintain an in-memory schema cache (LRU cache). On first encountering a schema, they perform an HTTP GET/POST to Schema Registry once and cache the mapping `(Schema <-> SchemaID)`. Subsequent millions of records reuse the cached schema in nanoseconds, eliminating network overhead.

option_explanations.A: False: Confluent Community Schema Registry is open and free to query.
option_explanations.B: Correct! Eliminates per-message HTTP latency bottlenecks.
option_explanations.C: False: Unrelated to TLS client certificates.
option_explanations.D: False: Avro parsing relies on cached schema objects for speed, not checksums.

questions.question: Which of the following actions constitute BREAKING CHANGES in an Avro schema under `BACKWARD` compatibility mode? (Select ALL that apply)

options.A: Deleting a required field that had no default value.
options.B: Renaming an existing field without an alias.
options.C: Changing a field type from `string` to `int`.
options.D: Adding a new optional field with `"default": null`.

questions.diagnostic_hint: Which modifications break deserialization when an old record is read with the new schema definition?
questions.explanation: In `BACKWARD` compatibility: (B) Renaming a field causes the consumer to look for the new name, which is missing in old records. (C) Incompatible type change (`string` to `int`) breaks binary decoding. (A) Deleting a field is actually ALLOWED in Backward mode (the consumer simply ignores it). (D) Adding an optional field with a default is the textbook definition of a COMPATIBLE change.

option_explanations.A: Allowed: Deleting fields is permitted in BACKWARD mode because new consumers don't need the deleted field.
option_explanations.B: Breaking: Without an alias, renaming appears as a missing field in old data.
option_explanations.C: Breaking: Binary decoders cannot convert arbitrary strings to integer primitives.
option_explanations.D: Compatible: Adding fields with default values is fully backward compatible.
